BEC 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert about someone's mailbox. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertSuspicious mailbox activity - possible Business Email Compromise. A user account signed in to the corporate email tenant from an unfamiliar foreign IP, and shortly afterwards that mailbox had an inbox rule created and external mail forwarding enabled.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated and cleaned up, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know whose mailbox was taken over, from where, what the attacker did to it, and what you have to do about it.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every click it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and a numbered circle points at the control.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole thing as a PDF.
One honest note, and it is a good one

The screen pictures are real screenshots of this lab, running Kibana 9.1.0. Every word, button, column name, row count and timestamp in them is what your own screen will show. The numbers in this guide are not predictions — they were read off these exact screens. If your screen and the picture disagree, stop and follow the If it breaks card near the end before you carry on.

There is no answer key in this guide

Not one line of it. Nothing here is filled in for you, and there is deliberately no "check your answers" card at the end. Your instructor holds a separate answer key and compares it with what you submit. If you cannot answer a question without opening Kibana again, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point.

The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

Microsoft 365The company's email and office system — mailboxes, rules, contacts, files. Everything in this lab happens inside it.
MailboxOne person's email account. Here it is kpatel. The mailbox is the thing that was taken over.
Inbox ruleAn automatic rule inside a mailbox: "anything mentioning an invoice, file it away". Ordinary users set these to tidy up. Attackers set them to hide things.
External forwardingAutomatically sending a copy of every incoming message to a different, outside address. Ordinary users set this up to read mail on a second device — if they still do. Attackers set it to read everything forever.
TakeoverSomeone who is not the user signs in with the user's password. The audit log cannot tell you the password was stolen; it can only show you the sign-in came from somewhere nobody expects.
Business Email Compromise (BEC)Fraud built on exactly this: take a mailbox over, then use it to redirect a payment or harvest correspondence, with the real user unaware. It is one of the most expensive kinds of cyber crime, and it costs almost nothing to attempt.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened: here, a source address, a forwarding address, a rule name.
True positiveThe attack is real. Contain it, clean it up, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* (Windows sign-in events) and cloud-* (Microsoft 365 audit events).
Data viewKibana's word for "which pile shall I look at". Older versions called it an index pattern.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 271 in the auth pile and 149 in cloud. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana's search bar. field: value means "field equals value", and and / or join conditions. This guide only ever uses KQL.
Audit logA record of somebody changing a setting, as opposed to using the system. cloud-* is an audit log. Where a mailbox is attacked, the audit log is where the proof is.

The five fields this investigation turns on

Almost every question here is answered by five fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • user.name — the account. kpatel is the one the alert names.
  • source.ip — the address the event came from. This is your pivot field, and the one you will be tempted to wildcard.
  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record, in the auth-* pile only. You need three of them:
    4625 = a logon failed  ·  4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4634 = an account was logged off
  • event.action — in the cloud-* pile, what was done. The two that matter are mailbox_rule_created and external_forwarding_enabled.
  • o365.operation — the same story in Microsoft's own words: UserLoggedIn, New-InboxRule, Set-Mailbox, UserLoggedOut. If you know one, you will recognise the other.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

A mailbox takeover always has the same beats: somebody signs in from somewhere they should not be, then they change the mailbox so it carries on working after they leave. That second part is what makes it dangerous, and it is the part most people forget to look for. Hold that pattern in your head.

first run is slowthen wait

The lab is a real Elastic Stack running on your own computer, hidden behind one file that does all the work. You start it once; it loads everything for you.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder — the folder that contains this guide.
  2. Find the setup file for your system and run it:
  3. On Windows: double-click setup-lab.cmd. A black command window opens and starts downloading Elasticsearch and Kibana. Do not close it.
  4. On macOS or Linux: open a terminal in that same folder and run ./setup-lab.sh. If your system says permission denied, run bash setup-lab.sh instead — that always works. To see what the file can do, run it with --help (a bare -? will not reach it: the shell swallows it first).
  5. Wait until it prints The lab is ready. and the two addresses. This is the slow part: 5 to 20 minutes the very first time, seconds afterwards.
  6. Your web browser opens by itself at the end, on the Security → Alerts page. That is the next card.
If the browser asks you to sign in

It will, because this lab's Kibana has security switched on. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing, and you sign in once. The alert you are about to read is already waiting on the other side of that screen.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification query 1 the failed sign-ins, a dead end = 46 query 2 the account's own sign-ins = 2 query 3 everything from the foreign address = 2 query 4 the whole mailbox audit trail = 4 query 5 the two mailbox changes = 2 query 6 the lookalike address = 31 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those six numbers are the spine of this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "cloud" index pattern cloud-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “event.code holds a number” and “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches. This matters more than usual here, because source.ip is an address field and not a text field — the difference costs you a query later.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — two of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

cloud-*cloud-*149Microsoft 365 audit: sign-ins, mailbox opens, sent mail, and the two configuration changes
Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The script notices the work is done and skips it. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and ruin your findings.

If you get a sign-in screen instead

This lab's Kibana has security switched on, so it asks who you are once. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing. Sign in and carry on; the browser remembers you for the rest of the lab.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Look at the Severity column. Both rows say critical. Look at Risk Score beside it: 99.
  2. Find the count in the donut, or in the Alerts by name panel. It says 2 alerts. That is two separate log records, not one summary.
  3. Read the Reason column on either row. It tells you the event was a configuration change, from 203.0.113.45, by kpatel. Write those three things down.
  4. Open one alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards.

What one alert says

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert's own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September at 10:07 and 10:09 UTC, which is the morning of the attack. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Open one alert on the Table tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-29T14:22:27.173Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:07:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today's real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules; ours is the only one you have, so it sits under Custom rules. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Find the rule called Inbox rule created or external forwarding enabled on a Microsoft 365 mailbox.
  3. Read its query. It is (event.action: "mailbox_rule_created" or event.action: "external_forwarding_enabled") — with no user and no address, because any mailbox changing its own configuration deserves a critical alert.
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your query count have to agree. The rule found 2. When Query 5 later returns 2 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

There is a second reason, and it is the better one. The rule is not scoped to kpatel. It is scoped to nothing. So when it returns two, that is not "two things about kpatel" — it is two configuration changes in the entire tenant for the entire day, and both of them happen to be on the same mailbox. That is a far stronger finding than a query that already assumed the answer.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The two alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, two critical alerts, risk score 99, both raised against configuration events from 203.0.113.45 for the account kpatel. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the mailbox, the address and the two minutes in which it was changed. What you do not yet know is why that address is signing in — and that is the next eight cards.

no typing needed

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks completely broken, and it is not. Here is the real screen, exactly as you are looking at it now:

Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

This build of Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language, and the Try ES|QL button is an advert for it aimed at people who already know their way around. It opens a screen with a query written for indices this lab does not have, and that query cannot work.

What to do instead: press the browser's Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

So what is wrong right now?

Two things, and only two: which pile of logs and how far back in time. The search bar is fine, Kibana is healthy, your account works, and the lab is not broken.

Learn the order of operations, because it is the order that works in every investigation: data view, then time range, then query. Fix them in that order and you will never stare at an empty screen for more than one click.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two, and the attack starts in one of them and finishes in the other.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it. It reads Default security data view.
  2. Look at the list that opens. There are only two entries that are yours, and this is what it looks like:
The two entries that matter, and what is in them
Data viewDocumentsHolds
auth-*271Windows sign-in events: successful logons (4624), failed logons (4625), logoffs, account lockouts, privilege grants, program starts
cloud-*149Microsoft 365 audit: sign-ins, mailbox opens, files touched, mail sent — and the two configuration changes that started this

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so a single entry covers every day of auth logs. If you ever see a third entry you recognise here, leave it alone and pick auth-*.

Why this matters more here than in most labs

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile — or, worse, it returns something and you do not notice the mistake.

In this scenario the mistake is unusually easy to make and unusually hard to spot, because both piles are about the same account. user.name: "kpatel" returns 2 in one pile and 4 in the other. Neither is zero, so nothing looks broken. Always check which pile you are in before you read a number.

If the sidebar says “no available fields” and stays that way

Then either the time range is still too narrow (next card) or the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

Be precise6

Open the time range to the right day

one click4 min

Right pile, and now the right time. The screen is still empty for one reason only, and this card fixes it for good.

Do this

  1. You should now be on auth-*. The screen says no results, and in the middle of it there is a blue button.
  2. Click the blue Search entire time range button. That is all — one click, and your records appear.

If you would rather pin the exact day by hand

Both methods return the same 271 documents, because every record in this lab happened on 22 September 2026. But if you want a fixed window you can type yourself, click the left half of the time range and the absolute editor opens:

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC, and every picture in this guide was taken on a computer set to UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your own computer's timezone, and no setting inside Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the inbox-rule creation that this guide calls Sep 22, 2026 @ 10:07:00.000 will appear in your table as Sep 22, 2026 @ 18:07:00.000, and your time range will read Sep 22 @ 08:05 → Sep 23 @ 07:59 instead of the two times in the picture above.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 3 minutes, then 4, then 2, then 3 — are identical in every timezone on earth.
  • The gaps are the evidence. The whole attack takes 12 minutes. Write the gaps down and you are right in any timezone.

Here is the one table you need if you want to convert a time this guide quotes. Find your own offset, then add or subtract it:

Your computer isExample citiesThen 10:07:00 UTC shows as
UTC+0Lagos, London in winterSep 22 @ 10:07:00
UTC+1Berlin, Paris, MadridSep 22 @ 11:07:00
UTC+2Cairo, Helsinki, JohannesburgSep 22 @ 12:07:00
UTC+5:30India, ColomboSep 22 @ 15:37:00
UTC+8Singapore, Beijing, Perth, Kuala LumpurSep 22 @ 18:07:00
UTC+9Tokyo, SeoulSep 22 @ 19:07:00
UTC−5New York, TorontoSep 22 @ 05:07:00
UTC−6Chicago, Mexico CitySep 22 @ 04:07:00
UTC−8Los Angeles, VancouverSep 22 @ 02:07:00

Not sure what your offset is? Compare the time range on your own screen with the two times in the picture above: 08:05 and 17:56 means you are on UTC. Anything else is your offset, and it is the same offset for every record. Or simply set your computer's timezone to UTC before you start — then every picture in this guide matches your screen exactly. Not required. But it removes a whole category of confusion.

The shape of the answer, before you type anything

Look again at that histogram: flat all day. There is no burst, no spike, no moment where the log volume says something went wrong. If you were waiting for a graph to tell you this story, it will not.

That is the real lesson of this lab, so do not skip past it. A quiet day is not a safe day. Six events in a flat 271-record log is a compromised mailbox, and the only way to know is to read the events.

Hunt7

Query 1: every failed sign-in that day

a dead endrun it anyway

Start wide, the way you would in a real investigation. The alert told you a mailbox was reconfigured; the most obvious thing to check first is whether somebody was failing to get into it.

Do this

  1. Data view auth-*. Type event.code: 4625 into the search bar and press Enter.
  2. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (46).
  3. Click the Field statistics tab, next to it.
Why running this query was worth it even though it found nothing

Because a big number with no owner is not a finding, and saying so out loud is a finding. 46 failed sign-ins reads like an attack in progress. It is six people having a bad Tuesday, and your report is stronger for having ruled it out in one query rather than quietly ignoring it.

This is the single most common mistake in a first investigation: starting with the number that looks scariest and building the story around it. The alert told you what to look for. Trust it.

The lesson, in one line

Rule of thumb: before you report a count, ask "of what?" 46 of 46 documents in this index. 46 spread across six accounts. Only one of those accounts appears in the alert. Two of the six hundred-odd log lines in this lab are the crime, and no count alone will ever tell you that.

Hunt8

Query 2: the flagged account's own sign-in events

the pivot4 min

Now narrow to the account the alert named. Query 1 was too wide; this is the same question asked properly.

Do this

  1. Still on auth-*. Clear the search bar and type
    user.name: "kpatel" and (event.code: 4624 or event.code: 4625)
    then press Enter.
  2. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (2).
  3. Read the two rows, and the event.code, event.outcome, source.ip and @timestamp columns.
What you have just proved

Not “a suspicious IP”. Something more precise: for this account, there are exactly two sign-in events in the whole day, they are three minutes apart, and the first one failed.

That combination is the textbook shape of someone trying a password and getting in on the second attempt. Now the only question left about the logon is whether that address belongs to the user — and the data view is about to tell you.

If this returns 0 documents instead of 2

Almost always the data view. Check the top-left control says auth-* and not cloud-* — the 4624 and 4625 codes only exist in auth-*, and this account has 4 records in the other pile. If the data view is right, check the time range still says 22 September and the Field statistics tab is not selected.

Read it properly9

Open one record and read every field

the habit that matters

Never write a finding off a table row you have not opened. One row here and the evidence for a whole part of your report is in the same place.

Do this

  1. On the auth-* data view, run user.name: "kpatel" and event.code: 4625 so there is exactly one row.
  2. Click the small ⇉ button at the far left of that row — the two diagonal arrows, immediately left of the @timestamp column. Clicking the row itself does nothing.
  3. A Document panel slides in from the right with every field and every value. Read it top to bottom. Press Escape, or click Close, to shut it.
Read the message field first, every single time

It is a free, plain-English summary of the record, and it is right there. A SOC habit worth building: expand the record, read message, then read the individual fields to confirm it. If the message and the fields ever disagree, the fields are what happened — and that disagreement is itself worth a note.

The fields worth copying into your notes
FieldValue in this recordWhy it matters
@timestampSep 22, 2026 @ 10:00:00.000When. The first event of the attack.
event.code4625It failed.
user.namekpatelWhose account.
source.ip203.0.113.45Where from. Your pivot.
host.namem365-tenantNot a workstation — the cloud tenant, not a laptop on a desk.
Hunt10

Query 3: everything the foreign address touched

is it ours?4 min

Query 2 gave you an account. Now flip it: ask what that address did, anywhere, for anybody. This is the pivot that turns a number into a conclusion.

Do this

  1. Data view auth-*. Type source.ip: "203.0.113.45" and press Enter. Note the quotes and note that it is the exact address, not a pattern.
  2. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (2).
  3. Look at the user.name and host.name columns.
The sentence this query earns you

“The address 203.0.113.45 appears in 2 of the 271 sign-in records for that day. Both belong to kpatel, and no other account in the organisation has ever signed in from it.”

That is a claim anybody can check, because it names the field, the value and the total. It is not “the attacker's IP was identified.” Write sentences like this one.

Now try the obvious thing, and see it fail

Most people’ first instinct is to widen the address rather than the account: “let me see everything from that part of the network.” Type source.ip: 203.0.113.* and press Enter:

Why that error is a gift, not an obstacle

source.ip is a real IP address type, not a piece of text. That means Elasticsearch stores it as a network address and will not do fuzzy things to it — no partial matches, no “anything starting 203.0.” An address has to be matched exactly, which sounds like a limitation and is actually a safety feature.

It is also why the setup script installed an index template before loading any data. Had it guessed, every address would have been stored as text, this query would have worked, and you would have lost the ability to ask questions like “which of these addresses is in our internal range?” Correct field types are not bureaucracy. They change what you are able to find.

To widen anyway, use a range: source.ip: 203.0.113.0/24 — no braces, just the network address and the subnet. It returns 33: the attacker's 2 records, and all 31 of the lookalike's. Read that number properly, because it is the whole card in one figure. A wider query is not a safer query, it is a different query, and this one has just handed you five ordinary colleagues who have nothing to do with anything. Narrow beats wide, every time.

Careful11

The address that looks the same and is not

the trap in this data

This data set contains an address that is one digit away from the attacker's and is used by ordinary staff all day. It is here on purpose, and it is the mistake this lab is built to catch.

Do this

  1. Data view auth-*. Type source.ip: "203.0.113.9" and press Enter. Look very carefully at what you just typed.
  2. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (31).
  3. Read the user.name column. How many different accounts?
Why this is the most dangerous mistake available to you today

Because nothing tells you that you have made it. 203.0.113.9 is a real address in the index. It returns real results. Your query succeeds, your screen looks healthy, and your report is confidently wrong — naming an address that belongs to five innocent colleagues.

And it is not a contrived trap. Addresses are read by humans, and humans misread them. Two addresses differing in one digit, in a data set where the whole case turns on which address it was, is a completely ordinary way for an investigation to go wrong. Real incident reports have been retracted over exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: copy the address out of the document, or read it off the screen twice — and if you are writing it in a report, read it back from the report before you send it.

A third address, for scale

There are only 8 distinct source addresses in the whole auth-* pile, and they divide cleanly into two groups: three inside your own estate (10.0.4.10, 10.0.4.11, 10.0.4.20 — the internal workstations in the sec-win-* logs) and five from outside it, four of which are shared by ordinary staff all day.

203.0.113.45 is the only address in the entire data set that belongs to exactly one account. That is not a coincidence and it is not a coincidence you had to be told about: it falls out of Query 3 in one click, and it is the single strongest piece of evidence in the lab.

Pivot12

Query 4: the whole audit trail for that mailbox

change pile4 min

Now change data view. Everything so far came from the Windows pile; the mailbox itself is recorded in the Microsoft 365 audit log. Switch the pile and read everything for the account — no filter on the event type yet.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown at the top left and choose cloud-*.
  2. Clear the search bar and type user.name: "kpatel", then Enter. No event filter. Everything for this account.
  3. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (4).
  4. Add o365.operation, o365.workload and event.action as columns from the sidebar.
Two things you should notice that are not in any of the columns above
  • There is no mail_sent row. Not one message was sent from this mailbox. Twelve other mailboxes in this tenant sent mail that day; this one sent nothing. The attacker did not need to send anything. They did not write a fraudulent email to anyone — they took a copy of everything that came in.
  • There is no mailbox_login row either. The other 25 Exchange records in this tenant are ordinary people opening their mailboxes. This account never appears in that list. Whoever was in this mailbox did not browse it. They signed in, changed two settings, and left.

Both of those absences are evidence, and both are the kind of evidence that only appears if you deliberately look for what is missing rather than reading the rows you expect to see. Say in your report that you checked.

Why you looked at the account, and not at the rule's query

Because you want the whole trail before you start filtering. The moment you add event.action: "mailbox_rule_created" you are asking “show me the thing I already know about”, and the two events around it — the sign-in that explains why, and the sign-out that proves it was deliberate and brief — disappear from the screen.

Establish the population first, then narrow. Four records is small enough to read; four hundred would not be, and then you would filter and accept the loss.

The core13

Query 5: the two mailbox changes, in full

the finding5 min

This is the query the alert was raised by, and the one your report is built on. It is also, character for character, the query your instructor's brief gives you.

Do this

  1. Data view cloud-*. Type, exactly:
    (event.action: "mailbox_rule_created" or event.action: "external_forwarding_enabled") and user.name: "kpatel"
    then press Enter.
  2. Read the Documents tab. It says Documents (2). That is the same 2 the alert page showed you, seven cards ago.
  3. Add email.rule.name and email.forwarding.target as columns. Those two fields hold the answer.

Now read the two records in full

A field name in a table tells you what happened. The expanded record tells you exactly what the attacker chose, and the choices are what make this provable. Click the ⇉ button on each row in turn.

Prove the pair is the whole population

Delete the and user.name: "kpatel" from the end of the query, so it asks about the entire tenant rather than one mailbox:

The rule's own query — run it by hand(event.action: "mailbox_rule_created" or event.action: "external_forwarding_enabled")

Still 2. That is worth more than it sounds: these two records are the only mailbox configuration changes in the entire tenant for the entire day. No legitimate user did this. Now widen one step further and see the context:

Why both changes survive the attacker logging out

Because neither of them needs the attacker to be there.

  • The inbox rule keeps running every time a matching message arrives. Finance replies containing the words invoice or payment are filed away and the real user never sees them. The user does not get an email saying "you are being scammed".
  • The forwarding keeps running for every incoming message, indefinitely. The attacker can be offline, asleep, or arrested, and the copies keep arriving at kpatel.backup@mail-exfil.example.

So the answer to “how bad is this, the attacker has gone?” is: it started 12 minutes ago and it has not stopped. That is the sentence that justifies acting on the weekend, and it belongs in your report.

Careful14

The same words in the other language return a different answer

silentcheck this

Kibana can read two query languages. This guide uses KQL. Switch to the other one and the exact same words return a different number, with no error and no warning.

Do this

  1. Stay on cloud-* with Query 5 in the bar. Confirm it says Documents (2).
  2. Click the ☰ button just left of the search bar, then the line reading Language: KQL, then choose Lucene. Watch what the tab says now.
  3. Put the cursor in the search bar and press Enter to re-run the identical text.
  4. Read the Documents tab. It now says Documents (4).
Why, and why it is dangerous

Lucene’s operators are AND, OR and NOT in capitals, and it has no parentheses. Type KQL’s lowercase and and or into a Lucene box and it does not complain — it quietly stops treating them as operators, so the filter collapses to “the account name” and the two extra records come back.

It fails towards more results, never fewer. That matters: a stricter-than-expected search makes you think there is nothing there, and you move on. A looser one makes you think you have more than you do, and you write it in a report.

Put the language back to KQL now, using the same three clicks in reverse, and confirm the count is 2 again before you carry on.

The one habit that prevents it

Before you write any number in your report, name the three things that produced it: the data view, the time range, and the language. “cloud-*, 22 September, KQL, 2 documents.” Four words, and nobody can ever argue with your figure — because you can be asked to reproduce it.

In this lab, all three are checkable in the same three clicks every single time. In a real one, they are in the URL of the search you are looking at.

Put it together15

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write six lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blanks are your work — read them off your table and type them in. The gaps on the right are pre-filled, because gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. fill in from your screen  →  fill in from your screen  (3 min)
    The first sign of the attacker. A failed logon (4625) for kpatel from 203.0.113.45 — the address nobody else in the company has ever used. A single failure looks like nothing. On its own you would never open a case.
  2. fill in from your screen  →  fill in from your screen  (3 min)
    Access granted. A successful logon (4624) for the same account from the same address — and, in the cloud pile, a UserLoggedIn audit record at the same minute. That is the takeover. Two piles, two records, one moment.
  3. fill in from your screen  (4 min later)
    The mailbox is reconfigured. mailbox_rule_created, New-InboxRule, a rule named Move to Conversation History matching invoice or payment in the subject or body. Four minutes. The attacker did not explore the mailbox; they changed it and moved on.
  4. fill in from your screen  (2 min later)
    The mailbox starts leaking. external_forwarding_enabled, Set-Mailbox, every incoming message from now on copied to kpatel.backup@mail-exfil.example. Two minutes after the rule. The two changes are a pair, not a coincidence.
  5. fill in from your screen  (3 min later)
    The attacker leaves. user_logoff, UserLoggedOut, same address. The session was nine minutes long and it achieved both objectives.
  6. fill in from your screen  →  still true now
    The attack does not end here. No timestamp. The inbox rule is still filing the finance replies. The forwarding is still copying every message to kpatel.backup@mail-exfil.example. Both are still running, and both keep working with nobody signed in.

The clock times above are UTC, which is how the lab stores them and how this guide's pictures were taken. If your screen is showing a different offset, write down your numbers instead — what matters is that the six lines stay in this order and keep these gaps: 3 minutes from the failure to the success, then 4, then 2, then 3. Twelve minutes end to end.

The shape of the answer

A flat, quiet day, and then everything in this lab happens inside 12 minutes at 10:00 in the morning. Strict order: a failure, a success, a rule, a forwarding change, a sign-out. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, and it rules out the user doing their own mailbox settings at lunchtime. A person tidying up their mail does not sign in from an address nobody else has used, fail, and try again three minutes later.

Then ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

These ten questions are the backbone of the report you are about to write. Answer every one of them in your own words, and write the query that proved it beside it — a claim with no query behind it is an opinion. The answers are on your screen, not on this page.

QuestionYour answerThe query that proved it
Who was taken over?
From where?
How did they get in?
What did they change?
What is the rule hiding?
Where is the mail going?
How long did they have it?
Did they send anything?
How far did they get?
Why is it not routine?

Two of those ten are traps, and they are the two the rest of this card has been warning you about: “from where” is a question about an exact address, not a partial one, and “why is it not routine” is a question about a ratio rather than a count. A number with no owner is not a finding, and neither is a count with no comparison.

Two things to check before you claim “one mailbox”

Have you actually searched the other accounts? Run source.ip: "203.0.113.45" on cloud-* as well as on auth-*. It returns 4 — the four records from Query 4, and all four on kpatel. Two queries, six records, one mailbox. Then, and only then, can you write “contained to a single mailbox” in your report, and that is a sentence an incident commander will be glad to read.

And have you checked the forwarding destination is not yours? If mail-exfil.example were an address the company owned, the whole finding would be weaker. It is not, and the domain name says why. Say so in one line.

The one-sentence verdict

On 22 September 2026 at around 10:00 UTC the account kpatel was accessed from 203.0.113.45, an address that appears in exactly two of the day’s 271 sign-in records and belongs to no other account in the organisation. Access was gained by a correct password, tried three minutes after a failed attempt. In the following nine minutes the attacker created an inbox rule matching invoice and payment and enabled external forwarding of all incoming mail to kpatel.backup@mail-exfil.example, then signed out. The attacker sent no mail and touched no other mailbox, but both changes are permanent and are still in effect.

That is a true positive Business Email Compromise. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the six queries you just ran. That is what a finished investigation looks like.

Deliverable16

Write the report, then export it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. Nothing here is filled in for you and there is no answer printed next to any of it. Fill it in from what you found, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a section in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These boxes are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. There is no model answer to compare against while you write; your instructor compares your submission with the answer key afterwards.

All three are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave any of them blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank. The verdict is a choice rather than a text box on purpose: a report that never says one of those two words has not answered the question it was asked.

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the data view and the language you ran it on, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning — and a number without an owner is not a finding

4. Impact

What is affected, and what is not

the mailbox, the address it was copied to, how long the copy is likely to have run, and — just as important — what you checked and found not affected. Do not overstate: “mail to one external address from your time” is defensible, “the whole tenant was breached” is not, and you have the evidence for the first and not the second

5. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line — the two words from the box above — then the whole chain in one paragraph, in the order it happened

6. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out, and for each one say how you would confirm it actually worked. Think about what survives the cleanup: changing the password does not remove the inbox rule, and signing the user out does not stop the forwarding. If an action needs to be done twice to hold, say so — that is the single most-missed step in this whole response

A hint on the recommendations, because this is where marks are won

Work through it in this order and you will not miss a step:

  1. Stop the bleeding. Remove the inbox rule and disable the forwarding. Do this first: everything else is worthless while copies are still going out.
  2. Stop the access. Revoke the user's active sessions and tokens, then reset the password and require multi-factor authentication. Revoke before you reset, or the attacker's session can simply be refreshed back to life.
  3. Block and hunt. Block the forwarding domain and the source address. Then search every mailbox in the tenant for the same rule name and the same forwarding destination, because an attacker who took over one mailbox has usually tried more.
  4. Establish the damage. Work out how long the forwarding was on and how much mail left. Then read what was in it: this mailbox belongs to finance, so the contents are the customer list and the payment threads.
  5. Close the door behind you. Alert on inbox-rule creation and on forwarding changes to outside domains, and alert on sign-ins from an address the tenant has never seen. That last one would have caught this at 10:03 instead of at 10:07.

Export it

The button builds the file for you out of what you typed — your name, batch number and verdict at the top, then your six sections, each under the label you filled it in against. Anything you left blank is written in as [not answered] rather than quietly dropped, so a hole cannot turn into a tidy-looking submission. The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Your finished submission
Before you submit, check all seven

If any of these is no, it is not finished:

  • Your name, batch number and verdict at the top of this card are filled in.
  • Every box has something in it — not a placeholder, your own words.
  • Your timeline is in order, every line has a time on it, and the gaps are the ones you measured.
  • Your evidence names the data view and the language for each count, as well as the number and what it proved.
  • Your summary would still make sense to someone who has never heard of Microsoft 365.
  • Your impact section says what is not affected, and you actually checked.
  • You have pressed EXPORT MY SUBMISSION, opened the PDF, and handed in the file.
Finish17

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have exported and submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container bec-mailbox-rule-001-elasticsearch container bec-mailbox-rule-001-kibana volume bec-mailbox-rule-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) file .../bec-mailbox-rule-001/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-bec-mailbox-rule-001

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates, the rule and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference18

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Three things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty, or it shows the wrong thing

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? Queries 1, 2 and 3 need auth-*; queries 4 and 5 need cloud-*. The lookalike address two cards back is an address search, exactly like query 3, so it needs auth-* as well — that is the check the setup file labels query 6, which is why its list ends on it. A 4624 query on cloud-* returns zero, and a mailbox query on auth-* returns zero. Both directions.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
  4. Is it KQL? Click the ☰ left of the search bar and read the bottom line. If it says Lucene, every count on this card is wrong.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today and the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the two come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
0 for query 2 or 3You are on cloud-*. The event codes live in auth-*.
0 for the lookalike addressSame mistake, the other way round: you are on cloud-*. It is a source.ip search, so it belongs on auth-*.
4 for query 5You are in Lucene. Switch back to KQL. This is the single most common wrong number in the lab.
4 for query 5 and you are sure it is KQLYou are on auth-* and the event.code text is being matched loosely, or you left the user.name clause off on a wider time range.
An error about a prefix query on source.ipYou typed a wildcard on an address field. Expected — read the card that shows the error.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the time-range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.
Every field starts kibana.alert.You are in the Default security data view, looking at the alerts instead of the logs. Switch to auth-*.

3. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says Engine running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run teardown.sh / teardown.cmd from the folder that owns it.
a container called bec-mailbox-rule-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run the teardown file from the original folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 271A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run the setup file with reset.
the rule is installed but has not produced 2 alertsKibana may still be starting its rules engine. Wait a minute and run the setup file again — it leaves an existing rule alone and only re-checks the alerts.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value. It will not give you “11 and 7” style counts — for an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Language is KQL? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all five are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return 46 documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text or the data view rather than in the dates.
